newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan warns aid groups to keep out of war zones.
newsitem.headline: Sudan warns aid groups to keep out of war zones.

text.p: Sudan on Sunday warned United Nations relief groups to stay away from areas in the south where government troops are locked in battle with the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA).

The official news agency SUNA quoted State Minister for Social Planning Major-General Hassan Osman Dahawi as saying relief groups operating in the fighting areas risked being considered supporters of the rebels.
The SPLA has been fighting since 1983 for greater autonomy or independence for the Christian and animist south from the Moslem and Arabised north.
The group seized the southern town of Yei, 160 km (100 miles) southwest of the southern capital Juba on March 12 and vowed to continue to Juba.

"The relief activity currently being carried out by U.N. specialised agencies including the World Food Programme and Unicef and other voluntary organisations at the military operation zones in the south is regarded as a flagrant violation of Sudan's sovereignity and the Operation Lifeline Sudan (OLS) agreement," said Dahawi.

Operation Lifeline Sudan, which groups U.N. agencies in southern Sudan, said in Nairobi on Thursday up to 20,000 people in Yei urgently needed food and medicine because of fighting when rebels seized it.

It said up to 1,200 prisoners of war as well as wounded soldiers also urgently needed food and medicine. The relief operation said roads were open for the first time in many years from northern Uganda to Yei following the rebel offensive.
The rebels said on Saturday they had captured an army garrison west of Juba, bringing to seven the number of outposts taken in two days.
OLS said while the logistics of moving aid by road into the south from Uganda were finalised the U.N. Children's Fund sent a planeload of aid to Yambio in the south on Wednesday for Yei.

The relief programme said two U.N. World Food Programme trucks with 40,000 tonnes of food were expected to arrive on Thursday in Yei and a team would visit the town to assess needs of refugees who trekked back to their home areas from northern Uganda in recent weeks.
Dahawi said some relief groups had not completed the procedure needed to get permission from the Sudanese government to transport relief materials to areas such as Yei and its surrounding areas.

"The use of planes and other relief transport means in the war zones is also regarded as illegal and poses a flagrant violation of the principles related to Operation Lifeline Sudan and could be viewed as direct support to the outlaw movement," Dahawi said.
He said the OLS branch office in the south had violated the principles of the relief agreement by issuing permission to a survey team to travel from Moyo in Uganda to Yei on March 28.
